QF.id: XIII Trading, Clearing, Settlement and Risk Management_48

question.text: Which statement correctly describes the brokerage ceilings applicable to exchange-traded derivative contracts?

answer.text: Brokerage is mutually agreed between member and client subject to the maximum permissible by the exchange and full tariff disclosure: for futures, brokerage cannot exceed 2.5% of the contract value (exclusive of statutory levies); for options, it cannot exceed 2.5% of the premium amount or Rs 100 per lot, whichever is higher
Brokerage in derivatives is completely deregulated — brokers can charge any amount as determined by market competition with no regulatory ceiling
SEBI fixes a uniform brokerage rate of 0.05% for all derivative transactions across all brokers
There is a single uniform ceiling of 2.5% of contract value that applies equally to both futures and options, irrespective of whether the consideration is the contract value or the premium

explanation.text: The Logic: Brokerage on derivatives is mutually agreed between the member and the client subject to the exchange-permissible maximum, with tariffs required to be disclosed to clients. The workbook distinguishes futures and options: for futures the ceiling is 2.5% of the contract value (exclusive of statutory levies), while for options the ceiling is 2.5% of the premium amount or Rs 100 per lot, whichever is higher. The Trap: Brokerage is not fully deregulated nor uniformly fixed. A single 2.5%-of-contract-value cap does not apply to options — for options the base is premium, with a per-lot floor of Rs 100 alongside the percentage cap. Note: Statutory levies (STT where applicable, stamp duty, GST, exchange and SEBI charges) are over and above brokerage. In practice, competition has pushed actual brokerage far below the ceilings, but the regulatory maximums remain the binding outer limit.
